questions.prompt: What is the main risk of RDB (snapshot) persistence?

options.text: It makes restarts extremely slow
On a crash you lose everything written since the last snapshot
It cannot be used for backups
It logs every command, so files grow forever

questions.explanation: RDB captures the dataset at points in time; between snapshots, recent writes exist only in memory and are lost if Redis crashes.

questions.prompt: What is the default appendfsync policy, and roughly how much data can it lose?

options.text: always — essentially no loss
everysec — up to about one second
no — potentially many seconds
AOF has no fsync policy

questions.explanation: The default appendfsync is everysec: it flushes to disk about once per second, so a crash risks roughly the last second of writes — a balance of durability and speed.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Redis persistence are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: BGSAVE forks a background process so the server keeps serving during the snapshot
AOF replays logged write commands on restart to rebuild the data
You can enable both RDB and AOF at the same time
AOF always restarts faster than RDB

questions.explanation: BGSAVE is a background fork, AOF replays commands, and both can be enabled together. AOF restarts are usually SLOWER than RDB because it replays commands rather than loading a snapshot.

questions.prompt: Which option gives effectively zero data loss on a crash (at the cost of speed)?

options.text: RDB with frequent save rules
AOF with appendfsync always
AOF with appendfsync no
No persistence

questions.explanation: appendfsync always flushes every write to disk before acknowledging, giving near-zero loss — but every write waits on disk, so it's the slowest option.

questions.prompt: The command that snapshots the dataset in the background by forking a child process is ______. (one word)
questions.explanation: BGSAVE forks a child that writes the RDB file while the main process keeps serving clients, unlike the blocking SAVE.

questions.prompt: Why is the AOF periodically rewritten?

options.text: To encrypt it
Because it only grows as commands are appended; a rewrite compacts it to the minimal commands that recreate current data
To convert it into an RDB snapshot permanently
To change the fsync policy

questions.explanation: Appending every write makes the AOF grow unbounded; BGREWRITEAOF rewrites it into the smallest set of commands that reproduce the current dataset.
